#904. Firing a manager is often more about maintaining the illusion of control

In an era of advanced analytics, deciding when to move on from a manager still seems to come down to vibes rather than logic

He’d run out of time, out of credit, out of chances.

This time of year, we live in permanent peril of hearing some version of the above proclaimed with unshakable confidence. Some soccer manager has been fired and it is universally agreed that it had to be done, that there was no alternative, that the club’s hands were tied by circumstance.

It’s all a bit weird, this broadly accepted yet totally unscientific formula for when a manager must – MUST – lose his job. It’s a sort of alchemy of vibes, and results, and the absence of other scapegoats, and the alternatives available. It’s like that old definition of hardcore pornography by a US supreme court justice: I know it when I see it.

Shall we talk about Michael Carrick now? Yes, here is where we are obliged to debate the beleaguered Manchester United manager, who has been at the helm during the Red Devils’ first dip into the relegation zone since 1986 yet somehow is also definitely not at fault. There is almost total agreement on the latter point, that United’s issues are structural and systemic and absolve Carrick of blame. Still, he’s gotta go, because what can you do, eh?

By the time you read this, he may be gone, or about to be gone, or still floating around in the liminal vapors of being emotionally, but not yet physically, gone.

He was caretaker manager and did such a good job at that free-hit, can’t-lose gig – five stars! Clean and comfortable ride! – that he was rewarded with the exact same but altogether more difficult job of being the permanent Manchester United manager.

But the discourse has shifted against Carrick. Suddenly, the exact same skillset that helped him rescue United last season, making him a poster child of club DNA and its virtues, is viewed as deficient.

Now they say Carrick is outsmarted by the other managers, overwhelmed by the volume of games. Perhaps. But his tactical mind was up to it last year. With fewer games to worry about, certainly, but also burdened with Ruben Amorim’s debris to clear away first. Amorim, of course, was the predecessor who Simply Had To Go, because he was dogmatic and would need too much time to instill his methods, after he was hired because the club must have quite liked that he was dogmatic, even though he would need considerable time to instill his methods.

Yet hanging on to a manager often works out. There’s the famous case of Sir Alex Ferguson, of course, who was installed during United’s last flirtation with relegation, 40 years ago. The early years of his reign were not always smooth: he had a poor season in 1988-89 and was reportedly a few bad results from being sacked in January 1990. But he wasn’t, and nine years later, he was knighted for his accomplishments in management and, by extension, in not being fired.

It’s true of Mikel Arteta, too, who has teetered several times in charge of Arsenal. When the now-defending champions started the 2021-22 season without winning or scoring in three matches, including a 5-0 humiliation by Manchester City. And in late 2024. And as recently as this spring, when some felt that if Arteta didn’t deliver the title at last, he ought to be replaced. Six months on, that seems unthinkable.

There’s a graphic doing the rounds on social media showing that Carrick has actually done slightly better than Arteta in his first 27 league matches in charge, although this elides the very obviously opposite trajectories they were on. All the same, Arteta got to keep going; Carrick probably won’t. Few managers these days are allowed to grow on the job, or into it. The very things Ferguson once credited for his longevity – the leeway to evolve and develop and learn from his mistakes, to rebuild and retool – are denied to the managers supposed to succeed him. Because of … reasons? The money was different back then, but the pressure wasn’t.

Instead, that predictable thing has happened where Carrick has morphed from the in-fashion manager to the one who is gently mocked. He’s no longer said to look calm and possessed of the desperately needed poise at a tumultuous club. Now, he is described as glum. It seemed an ominous portent that he should add himself to the ultra-niche lore of English managers misusing umbrellas when he promised to hold the umbrella so that he would get wet and keep everyone else at the club dry, possibly owing to an unfamiliarity with the rudiments of the technology.

Carrick isn’t alone in managerial purgatory.

Crystal Palace’s Pierre Sage: sacked but somehow not yet sacked.

Régis Le Bris: safe for now, in spite of taking newly promoted Sunderland to an astounding seventh place last season.

Newcastle’s Matthias Jaissle: medium rare, but not yet cooked.

Manchester City’s Enzo Maresca: definitely no longer the perfect successor to Pep Guardiola he was just a few weeks ago.

Fulham’s Álvaro Arbeloa and Bournemouth’s Marco Rose and Tottenham’s Roberto De Zerbi are fine now, after starting the season very not fine. That may change after any result at all. Because clubs’ decision-making on managers seems to be all just guesses and gambles. A veneer of deep deliberation is projected on to the process, because on the outside we always assume that soccer is more sophisticated than it is, but none of them really know which manager will perform in what situation, and for how long.

That’s amazing, given the advances in analytics and how much really rides on a manager’s ability to win games. Ballooning analytics departments seem to have taken teams to a place where they make far fewer mistakes in the transfer market than they used to.

Yet hiring a new manager, or firing the old one, or giving him another chance, appears to involve only marginally more design than shaking a Magic 8 Ball and seeing whether it endorses your choice.

Make a managerial move just to do something and appear in control? Signs point to yes.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#903. Hill insists Ferrari should back 'extraordinary' Hamilton over Leclerc

Catch up on all the major talking points from the Sao Paulo GP by listening to the latest episode of The F1 Show podcast; Damon Hill and Anthony Davidson join Simon Lazenby to discuss Ferrari's issues, Mercedes' completing their title double, and Lando Norris' victory in Brazil

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former Formula 1 world champion Damon Hill has insisted Ferrari should back the "extraordinary" Lewis Hamilton over his team-mate Charles Leclerc if they want to have a chance of winning next year's drivers' title.

Ferrari's handling of their drivers came under increased scrutiny earlier this month following the Mexico City Grand Prix when a first-lap clash between Hamilton and Leclerc, running in first and second respectively at the time, cost the Italian team a likely one-two, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen going on to win the race.

Hamilton, who had started on pole and led on the approach to the first corner, was highly critical of Leclerc after the race for what he perceived to be an overly aggressive approach against a team-mate. Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur also expressed his displeasure at the incident.

The seven-time world champion said any issues he had with Leclerc had been "squashed" following a conversation at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, which came the weekend after the race in Mexico.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hill, the 1996 world champion, wrote on social media following the race in Mexico that Italian squad should make Hamilton their number one driver for the 2027 season and that "Lewis will deliver for Ferrari if they back him 100 per cent."

Appearing on the latest episode of Sky Sports' The F1 Show following the triple-header of races, Hill explained his position.

"They [Ferrari] have invested all this in Lewis, they've got him on board, he is a massive name in the sport," the 1996 world champion said.

The F1 Show: What happened with formation lap at Bahrain GP?

Toto Wolff's claims that Mercedes can't afford to match rivals' 2026 upgrades assessed by Bernie Collins on The F1 Show podcast

Lando Norris: McLaren driver's hopes of chasing down Kimi Antonelli in 2026 F1 title battle assessed on The F1 Show podcast

Max Verstappen: Red Bull driver's options for 2027 switch assessed after 'frustrating' British GP weekend

Ferrari need to focus on Lewis Hamilton to have chance of winning 2026 F1 title, says Jacques Villeneuve

The F1 Show: FIA decision to grant pace-setting Mercedes engine upgrade questioned by Sky Sports F1's David Croft

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"If they have a competitive car next year, they could win the Drivers' Championship and the Constructors' Championship, and I can't see how they're going to win it if they have two drivers currently behaving the way they do, if Charles is constantly racing against Lewis like that.

"So, you have to make a decision as a team principal how you're going to enter into the fray. And I think it makes sense to me to put all your eggs behind Lewis.

"You've got him there anyway. You've gone through all the pain and the investment to get him there. It would be a huge story, clearly. His eighth world title is just sitting there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Now Charles might say, well, this is totally unfair, you know, I've been here longer. But yes, you have been there longer, but look at the results.

"Lewis has got a valid point, which is he's there to make them win as a team, not just be a Ferrari driver."

After claiming the most recent of his seven titles in 2020, Hamilton was controversially denied a record eighth triumph as he lost out to Max Verstappen at the final race of the 2021 season.

That coincided with a drop-off in performance for the Mercedes team that Hamilton had won six of his seven titles with, which ultimately played a part in the Brit deciding to make a blockbuster switch to Ferrari for the 2025 season.

Hamilton's last campaign with Mercedes and first with Ferrari suggested he was on the decline as he was outperformed by former team-mate George Russsell and then Leclerc, but he has returned to form in 2026.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

With the all-new cars for this season appearing to better suit him, Hamilton claimed his first grand prix victory for Ferrari in Barcelona to reignite hope he could once more contend for the title.

Leclerc, who spent just one season at Sauber before joining Ferrari as a 21-year-old, has claimed nine grand prix wins across his eight campaigns with the Italian team.

Hill added: "I think there's a gravitas that Lewis has. I mean, don't forget what he was like last year. He was crushed.

"He's been crushed since Abu Dhabi, in effect, you know, in 2021. He's been fighting his way back. He's performed incredibly well this year, much better than I thought, considering I thought it was going to be very difficult, but he's rebuilt himself.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"He is an extraordinary individual. And I think he has, and he's got pole positions and won races this year in a Ferrari. Who would have said that was possible last year?

"And I think we need to settle this in the team because there's a political problem in that team. For me, it seems like there's factions within the team that are shooting for one side or the other.

"You can't have that if you're going to be an effective competitor against the Red Bulls, McLaren and Mercedes."

Sky Sports F1 pundit Anthony Davidson, appearing on The F1 Show alongside Hill, questioned whether Hamilton has earned number one status over Leclerc at Ferrari.

Hamilton is fourth in the 2026 drivers' standings, a place ahead of Leclerc with just 12 points separating the pair.

Davidson compared the situation to that of Verstappen at Red Bull, where the four-time world champion has long received preferential treatment over his team-mates.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Davidson said: "Do you think, though, with Red Bull, that it's not like they give Max better equipment? He has, without question, earned that status in the team through his dominance of lap times alone.

"And it's pretty much every time. A bit like [Michael] Schumacher did against either [Rubens] Barrichello or [Felipe] Massa or [Eddie] Irvine.

"It was just every time he is unbeatable. And you earn that. You have to earn that status.

"I'm not comfortable with the fact, thinking of Charles, the speed he had particularly last year. I wouldn't be comfortable with the fact if you just say the number one in the team is Lewis and Charles, no matter where he is, you finish behind.

"That doesn't sit easy with me. I think to a certain degree, you have to earn that status in the team."

#901. Cerebral Josh King plots unusual route into Tuchel’s England plans

Armed with an impressive academic record and experience as a rugby fly-half, the teenager is anything but typical

Josh King is talking with pride about how his mother, Michelle, a university lecturer, has almost finished her PhD in sickle cell disease. The Fulham attacking midfielder, who is in the England squad for the Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain this week, mentions that his father, Steve, is a lawyer and says he might have liked to follow in his footsteps if it had not worked out for him on the pitch.

King’s background is not that of a typical footballer. Privately educated at Hampton School in south-west London, he aced his GCSEs, achieving A or A* in his 10 subjects. He went on to study part-time for A-levels in French, maths and psychology, getting grades of A, C and D – pretty impressive, especially when you consider he sat the exams in a hotel suite in Romania in the summer of last year while playing for England at the European Under-19 Championship.

Is there a link between King’s academic prowess, whether nature or nurture, and his success as a player? He thinks so and it goes beyond the basic eye test of what you see in his game – the appreciation of the spaces, the quicksilver cuteness.

“It definitely has an impact … I know my mum would probably say so,” the 19-year-old says with a smile. “The most important thing about being good academically and education-wise is you’re able to take on information much more quickly. You can almost take on information which might take a bit longer for other people. That definitely helps. It’s always been something that has helped me. Being able to communicate with my teammates, sometimes younger players, sometimes older players – it’s a massive part of football. Having those skills is really important.”

King’s rise has been rapid. He enjoyed his breakthrough season in 2025-26, appearing in 32 of Fulham’s 38 Premier League matches, starting 15 of them, and it led to Thomas Tuchel giving him a first England call-up for the pre-World Cup camp in Florida. King did not play in either of the friendlies but the experience was invaluable and motivating. This season, he has been an ever-present in Fulham’s starting league team and it is no exaggeration to describe him as one of the country’s most exciting teenage talents.

Tuchel has a wealth of options in the No 10 position: Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Eberechi Eze and Morgan Gibbs-White. He cannot find room for Phil Foden or Cole Palmer, as much as he would like to involve the former. But he wanted to see King during this camp and has noted that he can be an option off the wings; also as a No 9 in training. Tuchel even used King as a full-back during the sessions in Florida and, although he has promised not to do that this week, it is a further example of the player’s flexibility.

“There were a lot of people I learned from in Florida and Jude [Bellingham] was a standout,” King says. “He took me under his wing and really tried to make me feel welcome. Harry Kane did, as well. The main thing you take [from all the players] is the standards they set. The way they perform every day. The will to win, the competitive edge. Then there were the technical things – the way some people strike the ball, the way they pass. It was little things that you almost take without thinking but they have an impact.”

King was due to be in Florida on a family holiday because his mother was booked to speak at a conference about her PhD. He was delighted to make it a work trip of his own. “My mum is very close to finishing her PhD in sickle cell disease, which is a disease that usually affects the black and mixed community,” King says. “She’s an incredible woman, someone I really look up to. Her work ethic and the way she holds herself is incredible. She’s someone I strive to be more like.”

King’s influences are varied. In his younger days, he played as a rugby union fly-half. “That’s definitely contributed,” he says. “In terms of your movement, your ability to manoeuvre the ball, hand-eye coordination and foot-eye coordination … obviously as a fly-half, I used to do a lot of kicking. Football was always my passion and I was better at football. I would love to play a bit of rugby after my career because it’s quite physical. I don’t want to get injured!”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It is no surprise to hear King name the Bayern Munich No 10, Jamal Musiala, and the Barcelona playmaker Pedri as stars from whom he has taken his cues. He has previously spoken of his admiration for the Barcelona midfield great Andrés Iniesta. “There are a lot of players that I’ve enjoyed watching over the last years,” King says. “And one of them is in the dressing room with me now. Jude is incredible – the way he plays and conducts himself, his energy, his passion. His quality is really top. He’s someone I definitely look up to.”

King joined Fulham at the age of eight, roughly when Tom Cairney arrived from Blackburn and began to establish himself as a club favourite. King idolised Cairney; as an 11-year-old, he was a mascot and walked out at Craven Cottage holding Cairney’s hand. It is a nice detail of King’s story that he can now call Cairney a teammate.

“I’ve said it before but Fulham is like a second home to me,” King says. “It’s a club which really feels like a family to me. Being there throughout my career has been massive. I had a lot of coaches and some of them stayed with me as I came up. I remember one called Charlie Turnbull who I had for five straight years from under-10s to under-14s. Having that continuity of coaching and that place you can almost call home is really important for your development.”

On Episode 235 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Dr. Jim Green to talk about the past, present, and future of planetary exploration.

Robots have, and always will, be the first to go to the dark and scary places in space. For many years, Jim oversaw these missions for NASA as their Chief Scientist. This Week in Space covers the new space age. Every Friday we take a deep dive into a fascinating topic. What's happening with the new race to the moon and other planets? When will SpaceX really send people to Mars?

Rod Pyle is an author, journalist, television producer and Editor-in-Chief of Ad Astra magazine. He has written 18 books on space history, exploration, and development, including Space 2.0, Innovation the NASA Way, Interplanetary Robots, Blueprint for a Battlestar, Amazing Stories of the Space Age, First On the Moon, and Destination Mars

In a previous life, Rod produced numerous documentaries and short films for The History Channel, Discovery Communications, and Disney. He also worked in visual effects on Star Trek: Deep Space Nine and the Battlestar Galactica reboot, as well as various sci-fi TV pilots. His most recent TV credit was with the NatGeo documentary on Tom Wolfe's iconic book The Right Stuff.

Responsible for Space.com's editorial vision, Tariq Malik has been the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com since 2019 and has covered space news and science for 18 years. He joined the Space.com team in 2001, first as an intern and soon after as a full-time spaceflight reporter covering human spaceflight, exploration, astronomy and the night sky. He became Space.com's managing editor in 2009. As on-air talent has presented space stories on CNN, Fox News, NPR and others.

Tariq is an Eagle Scout (yes, he earned the Space Exploration merit badge), a Space Camp veteran (4 times as a kid, once as an adult), and has taken the ultimate "vomit comet" ride while reporting on zero-gravity fires. Before joining Space.com, he served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering city and education beats. He has journalism degrees from the University of Southern California and New York University.

Space.com is the premier source of space exploration, innovation and astronomy news, chronicling (and celebrating) humanity's ongoing expansion across the final frontier. #898. Manchester City’s Kerstin Casparij: ‘I love football – but it takes over your life’

Dutch full-back on relief of winning the Double and needing a ‘sense of normality’ while in the spotlight

Kerstin Casparij loves football, especially Champions League nights under the lights, but perspective is important too. “I would say football is my most important secondary thing in life, and I’ve found that such a refreshing way of looking at it,” she says before Manchester City’s trip to Milan to face Inter on Tuesday.

“It is so important to me and I love it so much and if I lose I’m going to have a terrible day, but my family’s healthy, my friends are healthy, I am, and I don’t have to worry about anything; I don’t have to worry about getting the food on the table. Being able to see things from that perspective makes it so much easier to stay the person I’ve always been.”

The 26-year-old Dutch full-back has had a phenomenal year, winning a first league title and FA Cup with Manchester City in her fourth season in England. Casparij was integral, having arguably her best season in the Women’s Super League, scoring three times and providing seven assists – the joint-most assists in the league with Aston Villa’s Lynn Wilms.

Key to her growth last season under Andrée Jeglertz was that “now I’m allowed to really play on almost the whole right side”, she says. “And I’m allowed to and trusted with pushing forward and taking risks in the final third.”

Like all team players, Casparij credits her teammates, but her contribution was recognised with a place on the Ballon d’Or shortlist. She finished in 24th place, the fifth-highest defender.

Being able to share these wins with her team outside the team is important too. They “work tirelessly to help me out”, she says. “Especially my partner, who is so invested in my career and has been such an incredible support and helped me out in more ways than I can count. There are so many incredible people around me and I’m just really happy I can give back to them as well, as much as I’m proud of myself for achieving it.”

Casparij’s authenticity, openness and playfulness have made her a fan favourite, not only at City but across the league. Her pun-loaded Instagram captions are as witty and self-critical after a defeat as they are sharp when City win. She is funny, shows fire on the pitch and is not afraid of banter with rivals, and is also a passionate advocate for the causes that matter to her, including as an LGBT Foundation patron and by sharing her experiences growing up with ADHD. Social media is a key tool for connecting.

“I always want to be me and I want people that I knew 10 years ago to now speak to me and be able to be like: ‘Oh you haven’t changed a single bit, you’re still the same person.’ I have a lot of friends outside of football and it gives you such a sense of normality because football, the industry, is not normal and we are not necessarily normal.”

The connection with people matters because it cuts through the abnormality. “We’re in the spotlight every three days at times. We’re getting judged on our performance, we’re getting judged on how we do our work, so I kind of need that sense of normality to make sure I don’t take things too seriously and really keep both my feet on the ground.”

Having a partner who isn’t fazed by what comes with being a professional football player and understands the schedule and lifestyle is a big part of that. “I absolutely love football, I love everything about it, but it takes over your life and it’s definitely taken over ours,” she says. “You need a partner that understands that and loves it and is like: ‘Yeah, let’s do this together.’

“I’m so grateful for her and am so appreciative of her. She’s got weekends off but she doesn’t really have weekends off because they all revolve around me. Life revolves around me a lot and I try to make extra effort to make sure she knows it’s about her, too. We’re definitely a two-person team here, but to have her support and know she’s always there, she’s a massive part of my football journey.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

That journey has taken her a long way from Heerenveen, for whom she made her debut at 15. Almost two years ago, when Casparij signed a new long-term City contract, she told the Guardian she felt she had unfinished business at the club. She wanted to win, so what did securing the Double in May feel like? “Incredible. It was such a long time coming and I’d been dreaming of that for so long.

“There was a big feeling of relief. We were very determined to win the league and I feel like we remained very calm for very, very long, pretty much up until the end. We just knew what we needed to do to get the job done and we made a big point of having a winning language. As a leadership team we started to talk about ‘when’ we win the league rather than ‘if’ to create an environment that believed and where everyone was going to do everything we could to win.”

Whether City can retain their title is the big question. They did not play in the Champions League last season and there were questions before this campaign over whether they could juggle the workload. After nine games they are top and unbeaten, two points clear of Chelsea, who drew 1-1 with Everton at the weekend, before their meeting on Saturday at Stamford Bridge. City look as formidable as ever in attack but earned only their second clean sheet in their 5-0 defeat of West Ham on Saturday. In the Champions League, they have three draws from three games as they get reacquainted with the demands of European competition.

Were they aware of the doubts some had in pre-season? “Late last season some were still thinking we were going to bottle it,” Casparij says with a smile. “We see it. I’m not going to say we don’t, because we all follow the media, we all have social media, but it’s not something that gets really discussed very heavily. But it definitely adds fuel to our fire …

“It also allows us, as a team, to keep innovating, to keep thinking: ‘OK, what can we change? What can we improve? Where can we get better? Where do we sometimes need to tweak little things? What does the opponent do?’ And that’s the beauty of it and the fun part because it never gets boring.”

#895. Manchester’s soulless content machine football clubs sum up post-imperial Britain | Barney Ronay

United and City dominate the news cycle with stories so strange and vast they threaten to consume the rest of the league

In Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it.

By the final whistle that wild 4‑4 draw at Old Trafford felt like a fitting endpoint to the opening quarter of the Premier League season. As we head into a 12‑day international break it is customary at this point to take a set of readings, to anatomise the season to date, to offer up a state of the Premier League address.

Five games since the last time we did this, not a great deal has changed. Brighton have maintained their luminous insurgent energy. The headline chart-breakers are Tottenham, up from second‑bottom to 11th. The official Home Office Spurs In Crisis threat level has been downgraded from Definitely In Crisis to Probably In Crisis A Bit Later On. Roberto De Zerbi no longer looks like a doomed and haunted cartoon caterpillar. Instead he looks like a feisty and fun haunted cartoon caterpillar.

Otherwise there has been only one story in town across that autumn segment. And that story is Manchester, and the extraordinary contortions of two contrasting, but deeply conjoined mega-clubs.

Manchester City’s run from October to November kicked off with the guilty verdict on almost all of their financial charges, followed by an adrenal victory at Anfield, and finally a run of three problematic league defeats. United have basically fallen through the floor in the same period: played eight in all comps, won one, and a point off the bottom of the Premier League table.

At the same time both Manchester clubs have dominated the news cycle, inexhaustible content machines, and the source of football-adjacent stories so strange and so vast they threaten to surge up over the seawall and consume the rest of the league.

It is necessary at this point to talk about Michael Carrick and whether he has been sacked yet (current answer: no). It seems likely that this will happen in the current break, once the designated replacement has been lined up. Another Manchester United paradox: only here, in the realm of the mid-season panic-sacking do we suddenly feel ourselves in the hands of a slick and well-practised machine. Stand aside. We’re old hands at this. Leave it to the experts.

But Carrick is of course essentially another bystander to the ongoing reactor core meltdown. He didn’t appoint Michael Carrick. He has done nothing surprising in his role as head coach, simply been the best Michael Carrick he can be, which is a Michael Carrick unqualified for this level of management.

Even the club executives captured by the TV pictures in insinuating close-up every week are essentially bit-part players, useful idiots for the regime: the director of football, Jason Wilcox, who looks every week a bit more like an office clerk trapped inside a hijacked foreign embassy trying to signal desperately with his eyes that he’s close to the edge and can someone in a flak jacket please appear at the fire escape window pretty soon. And the chief executive, Omar Berrada, who personally oversaw the Manchester City commercial sponsorship regime, and surely can’t be allowed to stay in his role at a listed company if the appeal against City’s charges is dismissed.

These are just the visible symptoms, not the cause. This is what happens when you run an institution where it is necessary to appoint people at significant levels who are willing to exist at a compromised level, who feel delighted to have the chance to run this organisation, even badly.

And by now it feels too easy to say the obvious thing. Manchester United have one competent but entirely self-motivated majority owner, for whom this has been a wonderful financial opportunity; and another owner whose only addition to the spectacle is to demonstrate the non‑transferable skills of the average billionaire.

We know this now. United are trapped in a cycle of self‑consumption. It is an ingrained, self-cannibalising decline, like a depressed post‑industrialised city in miniature. All that remains is rust, people and unspent heritage.

But it has also created something extraordinary in the past few weeks. Right now the Old Trafford match‑day atmosphere feels entirely unlike anything else, not just in sport but any other human activity at which you care to point.

The periphery is now enshrined definitively as The Event. Here is a man in sodden navy woollen menswear haunted by strange noises, striding the touchline like King Lear on his way to a golfing weekend. Here is the United crowd clamped together inside a clanky and leaking stadium, gripped by macro‑forces, shouting at the tides of power, a drama of alienation taking place just beyond the white lights around the lip of the stand.

The currents of energy are so mixed and nuanced. Who is cheering what? Where exactly is the love, the fear, the rage directed at this moment? Like all the best human dramas it is both sweeping and bathetic, thousands of human souls in that same shared space, all focused on an abstract idea, the act of faith and memory they identify collectively as Manchester United, while in front of them Harry Maguire trots about like an ageing police horse and Diogo Dalot attempts to play football with his legs on the wrong way round.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

To the unconverted, football can seem like a distraction, a silly thing, the society of the spectacle with the society part aggressively deleted. But there is still something noble about howling into this physical space, about expressing dissent, protest, rage, which is the opposite of so many things that are unsatisfying about the wider world: fakery, remote emotion, remote experience.

Take a look at the world that surrounds the team on the pitch: asset-stripping owners, branding overload, a club that is entirely committed to monetising your emotions. To rage at this thing is not just rational and human but an appropriate act of resistance.

This is where the autumn 2026 version of Manchester City also enters the picture. On the pitch City were muddled and unusually open in midfield during the 3-1 defeat by an excellent Nottingham Forest on Saturday. But something has changed around the club in this period, expressed most powerfully in that travelling support.

The urge to defy the independent tribunal verdict, to lean into being “villains”, has been a little baffling from the outside. It is hard to understand how truth, freedom, sunlight, the little man kicking against the pricks is compatible with swallowing the party line of an autocratic propaganda project.

But the space is more complex than that, the tension less linear. The City fans in Cheetos shirts waving inflatable mnemonic bananas, raising their fists to the world, have also become strangely captivating, persuasive, unexpectedly likeable.

Because this is also at bottom a protest against a world that feels beyond your reach. Forget the accounting regulation stuff and it isn’t hard to find plenty that is cheerless in the Premier League model, in the complete prostration of elite football at the altar of money. Whatever its source, no matter how muddled the logic, there is a base‑level majesty in this spectacle of defiance and collectivism.

If it feels addictive, moreish, impossible to look away from, then maybe this is because something authentic is happening in a world of fakery and illusions. The Manchester clubs feel in their separate ways like a version of their own city’s modern form, of the way post‑post‑imperial Britain has tried to create energy from inward investment or stripping its parts, selling its soul for some glass and steel high-rises and a tramline. It is a process that also includes turning supporters of a football club into product, a piece of staging, the trees on an architects drawing.

There is no obvious solution to this, no way of reversing that process given the selling off of land, control, intellectual property, just as it can seem like there is no obvious practical route towards the soft, comforting, previously attainable things Andy Burnham conjures up in his speeches about the future.

But it is interesting to see football directly confronting this alienation, expressing, however incoherently, that the only sensible response is a refusal to be silent. The Premier League is in its own way a perfect reflection of the nation, with its ailing but wealthy boomer generation, its lightweight pop-up entities filling the vacant spaces in the high street.

The other key story of the autumn period is of course Arsenal, who are basically London in the form of a football club, economically functional, geographically privileged, ticking along under its carefully curated restrictions. Is this the story of the season from here? Even with 28 games still to play it is hard to see Arsenal’s five‑point lead as anything other than a steady progression towards another league title.

At the same time every metric, from social media spikes to estimated TV figures, suggests that the event of the weekend was by some distance a theatrical but essentially meaningless 4-4 draw in the rain on Sunday night. Drink it in. Raise a fist to the world. Manchester has been the capital of English football for so long. It remains, even in a state of football‑adjacent crisis, its most potent spectacle, still able to provide a sense of something real in a post-real world.

#893. Bronze named in World 11 for record ninth time

Fifpro has invited players to vote for the Women's World 11 since 2015

England defender Lucy Bronze has been named in the Fifpro Women's World 11 for a record ninth time.

Bronze is one of five England players named, with Alex Greenwood, Alessia Russo, Ella Toone and Hannah Hampton also selected.

Spain defender Irene Paredes also features for the first time since her previous selection in 2017.

Zambia striker Barbra Banda, named in the team for the third time, is the only player in the side based outside England or Spain.

The World 11 - the only global football award chosen exclusively by players - was selected through votes from 6,511 female players from 64 countries.

Goalkeeper: Hannah Hampton (Chelsea, England).

Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea, England), Alex Greenwood (Manchester City, England), Mapi Leon (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Irene Paredes (Barcelona, Spain).

Midfielders: Aitana Bonmati (Barcelona, Spain), Alexia Putellas (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Ella Toone (Manchester United, England)

Forwards: Barbra Banda (Orlando Pride, Zambia), Claudia Pina (Barcelona, Spain), Alessia Russo (Arsenal, England)

Professional players voted based on performances between 4 August 2025 and 16 August 2026, with only those with at least 20 appearances eligible.

Voters were asked to choose the three players who had performed best in each position: goalkeeper, defender, midfielder and forward.

The goalkeeper, three defenders, three midfielders and three forwards who received the most votes were selected for the World 11.

The final place was awarded to the outfield player with the next highest overall vote total, regardless of position.

#892. Diego Gómez hits another stunner as Brighton beat 10-man Brentford to go second

Who can stop Brighton’s ­ascension in English and European football? They are setting standards, ­practices ­leaving almost everybody else ­trailing in their wake. A ­second‑place position in the ­Premier League would once have read like a glitch in a ­Football ­Manager ­session. Not in November 2026, where they appear the only team capable of throwing down any sort of challenge to Arsenal.

Under low winter sun, Brentford, an opposition to which Brighton are often, if lazily, compared, were ­swatted aside. If Keith Andrews’s team, and their fans at the Amex ­Stadium, could level blame at a couple of ­refereeing decisions, they received little chance of rescuing anything. Brighton squeezed them, toyed with them.

If Pascal Gross, scorer of a perfectly hit penalty, attempted to dampen expectations of a title challenge, his manager, Fabian Hürzeler, allowed fans to dream. “They should always be excited, it’s our job to make them excited,” he said.

A successful return to the Amex Stadium following five Brighton away trips, more than 5,000 miles on the road including victories at ­Manchester City and Getafe over the past two outings. Brentford returned to a stadium where they have never won in the Premier League. Normal service was duly resumed, any Brighton negatives coming in a failure to add to their first-half goals.

An up-and-under straight from the kick-off was a rare Brentford foray into the Brighton box. Bart Verburggen catching it on the full prefaced an easy afternoon for the Brighton goalkeeper. There are many further dimensions to ­Hürzeler’s team. Last week Paul Scholes, an unlikely ­progressive, declared himself an admirer of a “level of ­coaching” he suggested is ­unsurpassed in ­English football. “The one thing that is non‑negotiable is to always put the team first,” Hürzeler said.

Diego Gómez’s opener was not as spectacular as the halfway-line goal of the season against Crystal Palace but a beauty nonetheless. Caressing the ball first with his left and then with his right, he laid up a thrash past Caoimhín Kelleher. Its trajectory was unerring, unstoppable. Hürzeler revealed: “Yesterday, he changed to shooting with [his] left foot … I couldn’t see him scoring with his left foot. I asked him after where this quality came from.”

The path to a commanding win opened up. Igor Thiago did not last many ­minutes beyond his failed attempt to lob ­Verburggen. Scuffling in midfield with Chema Andrés, his shove was first ruled a yellow by the referee, Michael Oliver. In stepped the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell: “violent conduct” and “with force” was the verdict from Stockley Park.

Afterwards, Andrews was ­visibly unhappy: “We’ve lost two games and both when down to 10 men. So we need to analyse ourselves first. In both scenarios we can do better. In both scenarios the opposition player has been the one to provoke the situation.”

Infact, both Yehor Yarmolyuk and Vitaly Janelt were dismissed against Liverpool, and if Andrews rues such lapses of discipline he was more unhappy at the initial decision’s video-assisted overturn: “The game is in a state now of a place I don’t particularly like.”

Straying beyond the confines of his technical area in a manner likely to add him to Mikel Arteta’s “massive storage of images” of such breaches, Andrews asked his team to dig deep but Brighton’s dominance of possession became near-total.

Luka Vuskovic, ­serving ­previously as a deep-lying playmaker, won the penalty. Keane Lewis-Potter’s ­panicked response to a physical 18-yard box mismatch was to snatch at the ­Croatian’s shirt. Gross’s penalty was struck as truly as Gómez’s goal. “We need to be cuter,” Andrews said. “I take real pride in the way we defend set pieces and we need to do better because that wasn’t good.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andrews’s half-time ­adjustments, bringing on Yarmolyuk and Nathan Collins, was an attempt to protect Brentford’s goal difference. Brighton continued to pile on pressure, their ­possession share reaching beyond 75%. A set piece became Brentford’s sole route back, though Mathias Jensen’s diagonal into ­Verbruggen’s hands would not have passed muster in rugby’s Nations Championship.

Ironic cheers from the away end came when Brentford won a corner, and then another – rare excitement at Brighton’s defenders being asked to do something other than build an attack. The visitors’ fighting spirit at least sustained, though threatened to spill over. When Kevin Schade shoved ­Vuskovic to the ground by the touchline, another red card was a possibility, only for Oliver and Attwell to rule a yellow as sufficient this time.

Brighton’s push for honours and further horizons will require more than spectacular goals. “You see the Premier League, the margins, you look at the results – we are not ­getting carried away yet,” Gross said. “Every game we have to suffer a lot.”

Hürzeler, like Andrews constantly straying beyond the confines of his technical area, does not countenance any let-ups. When Brighton meet the unstinting demands of their coach, so many are left in their wing mirrors.

#890. Hoda Kotb Details Co-Parenting Change With Ex Joel Schiffman

Hoda Kotb gave an update on her co-parenting  dynamic with ex-fiancé Joel Schiffman, sharing it's now "more important than ever" to have daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, spend time with him.

Hoda Kotb is glad her ex Joel Schiffman will be there for their daughters today—and everyday.

The Today show alum to came a revelation about her co-parenting dynamic with the businessman—who she split from in 2022 following eight years of dating—after the two recently reunited to watch their daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, take part in their school's Halloween parade.

“Usually, my kids wave and try to hide," Kotb shared as she filled in for Sheinelle Jones on the Nov. 9 episode of Today With Jenna & Sheinelle, adding that time time, "They saw Joel at the fence and beelined. They were saying to their friends, ‘That’s my dad,’ because they don't see him as much.”

“Whatever makes you different is hard, if your dad’s not there,” she continued. "I think there are a lot of kids who can relate. People will probably say, ‘Do you have a dad? Where is your dad?’ People ask them that."

For the 62-year-old, that exchange became a "very meaningful" moment in her motherhood journey as she realized the value in encouraging him to come more.

"As the girls are getting older, having their dad there is much more important than ever," Kotb explained. "When I was watching them say that, I thought, 'Oh my gosh, come all the time, be here as often as you can, because it matters.'"

All in all, Kotb said she and Schiffman—who dressed up in matching deviled eggs costumes to go trick-or-treating with their kids later that night—had a "lovely" time on Halloween.

"It was beautiful," she added. "He was on cloud nine. We all hung out. We barbecued."

But while Kotb and Schiffman, 68, work together on co-parenting, she believes their chapter as a couple has ended.

"Joel is one of the best people I know, and he really is a great human being," the Emmy winner raved on a 2024 episode of The Jamie Kern Lima Show. "And I feel like I'm a pretty great human being, but sometimes two great human beings together isn't quite enough to make it work."

Besides, Kotb recently struck up a connection with a man she met on a flight, who her former co-host Jenna Bush Hager jokingly called a "cute boy."

"Here's what I think of my future relationship life," Kotb shared after Bush Hager asked for updates on the Nov. 9 broadcast. "As I am going through life, there is going to be a person who shares more than just the things that matter to me when I was younger. I want someone with a deep spiritual connection, a deep emotional connection."

Though Kotb has admittedly been "scared" to date, she understands that she has to "take risks" in order to find love again.

"I‘m just keeping it as a thing," she added, "but truly, if I were to swallow a truth pill right now...I believe that the love part of my life is a piece that’s coming."

For now, read on to see Kotb's sweetest moments with her kids.

Life can leave its mark on a planetary atmosphere, so learning what properties are the product of non-life will help astronomers identify those worlds that might have life.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe.

Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life.

"The model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," Gilbert-Janizek, who was a PhD student at the University of Washington when the research was conducted, said in a statement.

Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. This new model pushed the simulation two steps further by incorporating the surface and atmosphere of the planet as well.

In all, the model simulates 19 properties of a rocky planet that are not related to life, including the amount of heat a planet receives from its star, the exchange of heat and chemicals from the core to the surface, and the outflow of certain gases from the subsurface.

Gilbert-Janizek’s starting point was to simulate the development of Earth had life never arisen here, therefore providing a baseline with which to compare to exoplanets. She ran the simulation from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future. The result was a lifeless world, but one that still had oceans and an atmosphere.

"When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface," said Gilbert-Janizek.

What makes the simulation especially useful is its plug-and-play nature. Researchers can simply apply the bulk properties of whichever planet they are studying to the model, and then just let it run. If the result is a planet with an atmosphere that matches what is detected spectroscopically by the James Webb Space Telescope or, in the future, the various extremely large 30-meter-plus ground-based telescopes or NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, then we know that planet probably does not have life as we know it.

However, if the simulated planet without life does not match what we observe on the real planet, then it becomes possible that life is present and altering the atmosphere.

"Dr Gilbert-Janizek’s work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,” said Barnes. "After more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earth’s core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate."

While any deviation from what is predicted by the model will not necessarily mean there is definitely life on a planet, it will help pick out those worlds that are worthy of follow-up studies by the next generation of telescopes.

Gilbert-Janizek’s model is described in a paper published in The Planetary Science Journal.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#888. Injuries, noise & scalps - Wrexham's season so far

Wrexham are competing in the Championship for the second consecutive season under Phil Parkinson

With 15 games of the Championship season gone, Wrexham have steadied the ship.

Phil Parkinson's side responded to a run of three defeats in four matches by claiming four points from their home double header with promotion-hopefuls Middlesbrough and Wolverhampton Wanderers.

It ensured they entered the final international window of 2026 in positive spirits.

As the club action takes a two-week break, BBC Sport Wales looks at the highs and lows of the Red Dragons' season to date.

So how does Wrexham's performance so far this term compare to the same stage last season?

Wrexham's performances in the draws with Cardiff City and Watford early on were encouraging.

They made light work of dispatching strugglers Preston North End and have earned highly-impressive wins against top sides including Millwall, Southampton and Middlesbrough.

Defensively, Wrexham's expected goals (xG) faced of 18.17 is the fourth-best in the division.

They have also made just one error leading to a goal, the joint-best return alongside four other teams in the Championship.

Up front, Kieffer Moore - who scored 13 times for the Red Dragons in all competitions last season - has netted five goals so far this term, in addition to claiming two assists.

The Wales international's return comes from an xG figure of just 3.23, meaning he has outperformed his xG by 1.77. He has also won 68 aerial duels, with only four players in the league managing more.

Others such as Jacques Ekomie, Issa Kabore, Ben Whiteman, Joe Worrall and Callum O'Hare have shown real glimpses of settling in after joining on permanent deals in the summer.

Amid the increasing noise surrounding the club's struggles earlier on, Parkinson yet again demonstrated an impressive ability to remain grounded and get his side back on track.

In terms of the league standings, Wrexham sit six points adrift of the Championship play-off places and eight clear of the relegation zone.

So there is plenty of reason for the Wrexham faithful to remain optimistic.

A shock departure and key results - inside Wrexham's seismic week

Wrexham owners' presence uplifting - Parkinson

Parkinson 'pleased' with point against Wolves

When it comes to the numbers, only five teams have a lower xG total than Wrexham's figure of 16.80, while only three sides have managed fewer than their 50 shots on target.

Wrexham's four through balls made is - alongside Lincoln City - the joint-lowest in the division.

Home defeats by Birmingham City and West Bromwich Albion were particularly underwhelming, while the 6-0 thrashing at West Ham United represented a real low point.

Following the 2-0 loss to Blackburn Rovers in October, former Wales international Nathan Blake suggested Wrexham were losing their "fear factor" and that they were in danger of becoming "ordinary".

The Red Dragons then produced a lacklustre display as they were beaten 1-0 by Sheffield United.

It promoted a strong response from Parkinson who said he and his players would not shy away from any criticism.

After the draw with Wolves, midfielder Lewis O'Brien said of the post-Blades debrief: "I think we had to look at ourselves, deep down. It was a tough couple of days."

On the back of the 1-1 draw with Wolves, which came three days after an impressive 2-0 win over Boro, Parkinson declared his side had needed a reboot following the defeat by the Blades.

"We've had a bit of a reset this week in terms of what the performances need to look like for our supporters and everybody at the club," said the manager.

"We know we've got the capabilities to win games, but like everybody, you can easily have a capability to lose a game and you've got to be right at it.

"There's no 80% scenario in this division, everybody's got to be at it, focused and ready, and we really were ready in these two games. We can take a lot of credit from that."

Injuries certainly have not helped the club's cause, while there have been several off-the-field issues too.

The Red Dragons have been fined twice fielding ineligible players.

Chief executive officer Michael Williamson departed last week, with Shaun Harvey taking over as acting CEO.

It has clearly impacted the club's efforts in the opening third of the season.

"You always have things going on in football clubs, it's never smooth running anywhere," Parkinson said after the Wolves draw.

"But I think this has been particularly disjointed, for various reasons."

Ben Sheaf, Max Cleworth and George Thomason have all returned to action in recent weeks following significant spells on the sidelines through injury.

Nathan Broadhead is also closing in on a return, although it remains to be seen when last season's top scorer Josh Windass, Callum O'Hare and Liberato Cacace will be available.

Discussing the November international window, Parkinson said: "It's a chance to get some work in the lads who need to work and build on what we've done this week."

Unfortunately, Sam Smith is set to miss the remainder of the season and will undergo surgery this week after sustaining a serious knee injury at Sheffield United.

It will likely prompt the Red Dragons to scour the transfer market for an additional frontman in January given that Bailey Cadamarteri is the only other option behind first choice striker Moore.

Davis Keillor-Dunn could also potentially be recalled from his season-long loan spell at League One side Sheffield Wednesday - where he has scored five times in 11 appearances.

But the outlook on the campaign overall has certainly improved in the past week.

Wrexham fans hope more progress can be made over the coming months.

#887. Crystal Palace poised to sack Pierre Sage and target Frank after Liverpool defeat

Frenchman under pressure after four successive defeats

Former Spurs manager Frank emerging as main candidate

Crystal Palace are poised to sack Pierre Sage after Sunday’s defeat by Liverpool left them bottom of the Premier League for the first time since December 2017, with Thomas Frank emerging as the main candidate to succeed him.

The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has been under mounting pressure since a 5-0 defeat by Brighton last month. There have been few signs of improvement as Palace have slumped to four successive league defeats.

Sage has guided Palace to only two wins from their 10 Premier League games this season and they have the league’s worst defensive record, with 24 goals conceded so far. Although there were promising moments during the 3-1 defeat by Liverpool at Selhurst Park on Sunday, their habit of conceding goals from set pieces has not been rectified and it is understood the patience of the club’s hierarchy has worn thin despite Sage only being at the helm for 16 matches.

He is expected to become the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season on Monday. Palace are already believed to have started the process of bringing in his replacement. Frank, who was dismissed by Tottenham in February, spoke to Palace in the summer and is said to be keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford.

The former Nottingham Forest manager Sean Dyche also has his backers at Palace and would be seen as a safe pair of hands given his vast experience in the Premier League. Vítor Pereira, another former Forest manager, could be an alternative.

Sage signed a three-year contract in south London after leaving Lens, where he won the Coupe de France and qualified for the Champions League in his final season. Palace have lost their two main central defenders this year, Marc Guéhi moving to Manchester City in January and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea in the summer. Two loan players – Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor – were signed as replacements. Palace did not land one of Sage’s top targets, Malick Fofana.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sage denied after the Liverpool game that his dream job had turned into a “nightmare” but suggested that Palace’s squad needed investment in January. “We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions,” he said.

#886. Metascience should be a source of evidence, not a means of control

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Efforts to apply metascience to research funding must put evidence and scientists front and centre.Credit: Alamy

The European Research Council made headlines last month when the news broke that those applying for one of its core grants had only a 5% chance of success. Partly as a result of applicants using artificial intelligence, the ratio of submissions to grants at the European Union’s premier science funder is now so skewed as to be little more than a lottery. Some funders are already using lotteries to select grant recipients, viewing these as a fairer way to allocate funding.

More self-reflection in research can lead to better science

More self-reflection in research can lead to better science

This is not a coincidence. The idea of distributing certain types of grant randomly has been tested experimentally over a number of years. It’s one example of how the field of metascience — the study of the practice of science itself — is having a real-world impact.

Metascience is not new. The world’s oldest journal devoted to the study of science, Nauka Polska, based in Poland, was founded in 1918 and is still publishing. Nature frequently reports on metascience, invites researchers to share their opinions and publishes primary science in the field. A set of studies released in April, for example, investigated the reproducibility, replicability and robustness of research in the social and behavioural sciences1–4. Developments in research funding, research organization, communication and evaluation are all aspects of metascience.

Metascience is also used by governments to support policy and funding decisions. In the past few years, a number of governments have established and funded metascience research units, as detailed in Seize the Meta Moment, a review by an international group of researchers and policymakers that was published last week by the Research on Research Institute in London (see go.nature.com/4z7pdt1). The author list includes members of some of these government-funded metascience units.

Huge meta-research project puts claims in social-science papers to the test

Huge meta-research project puts claims in social-science papers to the test

In one sense, this is positive, an example of policymakers seeking solutions informed by research. But the review’s authors point out that political attention also introduces risks — namely that the discipline could be misused to serve government agendas or to justify decisions that are not supported by a consensus of the evidence. They acknowledge that metascience will, to some extent, always be political, but that this should be acknowledged. And they urge politicians to use metascience as a learning tool and a source of evidence, but not as a means of controlling researchers.

In the United States, the Office of Science and Technology Policy has tasked all federal science agencies with establishing metascience capabilities. This was outlined in a July report, Science: A New Golden Age, which criticized excessive bureaucracy and slowness in US science, and embraced the idea of accelerating grant-awarding processes (see go.nature.com/3uj6pf5). One concern is that the US administration could use metascience to push through major changes, such as funding cuts, support for higher-risk research or the adoption of AI, without engaging the broader scientific community.

I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know

I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know

The United States is not the only country where researchers are worried about potential metascience misuse; concerns have also been raised in the United Kingdom, the first country to establish a government metascience unit. Last year, the nation’s main public funder of social science, the Economic and Social Research Council, announced a commitment to promoting economic growth. This is part of a broader economic push by the nation’s main public funder, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), in response to a government priority.

The extent to which publicly funded science contributes to growth and the mechanisms underlying it are well-studied questions in the social sciences, and there are a range of views both supporting and critiquing the UK government’s objectives. It’s important that funders such as UKRI do not align themselves with just one view, and that the metascience unit does not reduce measurement of grant recipients’ performance to a metric that is itself still a matter of debate in the research community.

Why science has a credibility problem — and how to address it

Why science has a credibility problem — and how to address it

Most of the world’s science funding agencies were established when research careers were accessible to relatively few people. There is now a much larger and more mobile pool of researchers due, in part, to the expansion of universities and the globalization of science. Funding agencies need to change how they work to adapt as the world changes. That includes addressing the problem of falling success rates resulting from the greater demand for grants.

By far the best way for policymakers to use metascience to inform funding decisions is for them to work with researchers to create and implement tools designed to measure quality and competitiveness, and — as in science itself — to learn from experimentation and experience.

#885. Kane and Bellingham air strong views in England World Cup review

Kane and Bellingham made their views clear at the review

England players are understood to have aired strong views about their World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in a team meeting.

As BBC Sport reported in September, the Football Association (FA) process included canvassing the opinions of the squad - and it has emerged that took place at a 'full and frank' meeting with head coach Thomas Tuchel at the start of the September international break.

BBC Sport has been told the squad feel that now they have been able to have their say, they can move on from their heartbreak in Atlanta on 15 July.

And this was demonstrated in the last international break when England, after a narrow defeat by Spain in the first game, went on to win the next three matches impressively.

Burn replaces injured Guehi in England squad

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

The ramifications of the Argentina defeat, or perhaps more pertinently, the circumstances, meant some of the squad held grievances, with those feelings lingering and even growing throughout the summer.

In particular there was unhappiness about how Tuchel told them to approach the closing stages of the game after Anthony Gordon had given them a 55th-minute advantage.

Enzo Fernandez struck an equaliser with five minutes left, before Lautaro Martinez headed in a stoppage-time winner.

As reported by BBC Sport at the time, a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive.

Hindsight, of course, is 20/20. England appeared to retreat in the closing stages of the last-16 tie against Mexico earlier in the tournament - but successfully defended a 3-2 lead to reach the quarter-finals to trigger scenes of joy at the iconic Azteca Stadium.

Nevertheless, certain players felt let down by the team's apparent pragmatism during the closing stages of the loss to Argentina amid a sense that going for the South Americans' jugular would have provided greater success.

Inevitably, the game against Argentina emerged as a key theme at the squad discussion.

It is understood that Tuchel pointed to the quality of the opposition as a key factor on why they eventually succumbed to two late Argentina goals.

There is, of course, merit to that argument. Lionel Messi was in the opposition team after all.

That said, it was not an argument the players in the meeting were prepared to universally accept.

There is a strongly held view within the England squad that their team, man-for-man, was superior to Argentina, who had 38-year-old Nicolas Otamendi on the field for the closing 18 minutes of the game.

All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting.

As you would expect, captain Harry Kane was strong and forthright with his views.

Jude Bellingham, too, is said to have been particularly candid in expressing his belief that this current crop of England players were more than capable of continuing to take the game to Argentina.

Bellingham's contribution to the meeting is said to have underlined his growing influence within the England squad, with many believing the Real Madrid midfielder will become the team's captain once Kane is no longer in the picture.

If the air needed to be cleared after the World Cup then it appears those honest discussions at the end of September did the trick.

Barring the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley in their first Nations League fixture in September, England have bounced back from the loss to Argentina emphatically - scoring 12 goals without conceding in three fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Similarly, the fluctuating relationship between Bellingham and Tuchel seems to have improved, too.

"It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place," Tuchel said last week.

"I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways."

We will get a clearer idea of how 'Tuchel 2.0' is progressing in the next few days when England host Croatia on Thursday and travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday.

#884. NWSL playoffs scheduling snafu: Washington Spirit keep Audi Field; Gotham move to Icahn

Washington to play in Saturday noon broadcast window

Shift to Northwest Stadium was reportedly in play

Gotham move to Icahn amid ‘atrocious’ pitch conditions

The Washington Spirit will play their NWSL semi-final at Audi Field after the club reached a deal to avoid playing a playoff game at Northwest Stadium, home of the NFL’s Washington Commanders. Top-seeded Gotham FC, meanwhile, will play their game at the 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium on Randall’s Island in New York City because of poor pitch quality at Sports Illustrated Stadium, their usual home.

The Spirit will play their semi-final against the Utah Royals on 14 November (Saturday) at noon, while Gotham FC will host the Kansas City Current on Sunday at 3pm.

The NWSL has had to maneuver through significant venue-availability conflicts in the past few days, balancing two sought-after national television broadcast windows with issues at the stadiums of the semi-finalists with home field advantage. Many of the teams in the league are not the primary tenants or owners of their stadium, meaning they are not able to exert full control or say over scheduling or conditions.

Audi Field has been the Spirit’s full-time home since 2023, and it has hosted raucous crowds for the team’s playoff runs, including Sunday’s 4-1 win over the Portland Thorns to advance to the semi-final.

However, a Division III college football game between the Coast Guard Academy and the Merchant Marine Academy was scheduled to be played at Audi Field on Saturday afternoon, a national TV window that the league would not be willing or able to move.

ESPN reported earlier this week that the NWSL had been preparing scenarios that would see the Spirit play their playoff game on Saturday at Northwest Stadium, a 64,000-seat venue in Landover, Maryland, roughly 10 miles north-east of downtown Washington where the team have never played a game in their 14-year existence, in the event that both the Spirit and top-seeded Gotham advanced to the semi-finals.

The Spirit are not the primary tenants at Audi Field. The stadium is owned and operated by MLS team DC United. The Spirit would not confirm if the college football game has been moved to a different location or date. As of Monday afternoon, it was still listed for its original time of 1pm on Saturday on both schools’ websites.

The location of Gotham’s semi-final against Kansas City was announced Monday afternoon. Though Sports Illustrated Stadium was available for the Sunday slot, the primary cause for concern was the state of the pitch. It has taken much wear-and-tear after hosting soccer and rugby matches in recent weeks, and would have hosted the semi-final just one day after MLS’s New York Red Bulls, the stadium’s owners, play a friendly against Liga MX side Club América.

During Gotham’s 1-0 win over Seattle in their quarter-final on Sunday afternoon, the venue’s field was patchy and sandy, with many visible brown spots. Reign captain Jess Fishlock described the field as “atrocious”. Gotham coach Juan Carlos Amoros apologized for the conditions and said the club attempted to mitigate the circumstances without success.

“Let’s be real, there’s no way a playoff game should be played on that shit,” Reign head coach Laura Harvey told ESPN. “I just can’t believe they’ve allowed it. They knew it last week.”

The league reportedly fined Gotham $10,000 for the poor conditions in their regular-season finale game on 4 November.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

“We as a team worked extremely hard to earn a home playoff berth. What we got was a field that is not the standard this club, this league or our fans deserve,” Gotham captain Tierna Davidson said in the club’s news release about the game relocation.

Icahn Stadium mostly hosts track events and is not well-trafficked, but has a natural grass pitch funded by MLS club New York Cit FC in 2024. It has hosted Gotham games in the past, including a regular-season match in July. Its capacity, though, is just less than half of Gotham FC’s average attendance this season.

“This was an extremely difficult decision, and one we did not take lightly,” said Yael Averbuch West, the president of soccer operations for Gotham FC, said in a statement. “After thoughtful consultation with coach Juan Carlos Amorós, our team captains and our ownership, we felt it was important to prioritize a playing surface that appropriately allows our athletes to perform at their best.

We fully understand and appreciate the impact this has on our fans, and we are equally disappointed that we won’t have the opportunity to play in front of more of our supporters at our home stadium. Unfortunately, we were faced with a difficult situation, and at the end of the day, the game is played on the field.”

#883. James Gunn and Peter Safran Leaving as DC Studios’ Co-CEOS

Four years after taking up the mantle as the head of DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran announced they are stepping down at the end of November.

It’s a bird! It’s a plane! It’s yet another shakeup at DC Studios!

Four years after James Gunn and Peter Safran were announced as the new heads of DC Studios—overseeing the line up of DC films, TV and animation—the dynamic duo announced they are stepping down at the end of November following the purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery by Skydance. They will be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham.

“Oh, boy. What a four years,” Gunn posted to Instagram Nov. 9. “Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios.”

The Superman director shared it was “a dream come true” to oversee DC’s super-powered slate of characters like Superman, Batman and Supergirl, saying it was truly a “unique opportunity” he couldn’t say no to.

Of course, with the “highest of the highs”—like directing the upcoming Man of Tomorrow and working alongside Safran—the 60-year-old also revealed that only those closest to him know that the past four years have also “been trying, to say the least.”

“I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that),” he added. “I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and l've stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.”

Gunn also had a special note for the wonder woman in his life, wife Jennifer Holland, writing, “Jenn, I love you and I'm sorry and you don't need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I'm no longer doing this job.”

And while he will “miss the people around” him and the heroes he got to be “co-caretaker” of, he is ready to release a new issue of his career and “get back to pure filmmaking.”

Still, saying goodbye to DC Studios does not mean ending the run of his upcoming projects, as he clarified that he is still working on a secret DC project in addition to Man of Tomorrow and producing Batman: Part II and the TV series The People v. Gorilla Grodd.

As for Latcham, who is taking up the mantle from Gunn and Safran—who themselves took over for previous DC head Walter Hamada—he has a history in the comics world, serving as producer on Iron-Man, The Avengers and Guardians of the Galaxy, which Gunn directed before being fired by Marvel over past offensive tweets.

“The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility,” Latcham shared in a Nov. 9 press release, “that I do not take lightly.”

And Gunn and Safran were thrilled Latcham answered the Bat-signal, adding in the release, “We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans.”

With Man of Tomorrow on the horizon for 2027, keep reading for more films hitting the big screen next year.
